faqs.q: How much should I expect to pay for wildlife removal in Philadelphia?
faqs.a: It depends on the animal, how it got in, and how much sealing and cleanup the house needs afterward. Row homes add a wrinkle: shared walls and connected rooflines can mean more entry points than a single house shows from the street, and sealing sometimes has to account for the neighbor's side too. Our crew inspects first, shows you the entry points we found, and gives you a quote after inspection before any removal or sealing work begins — no prices promised over the phone.

faqs.q: Can a raccoon in Philadelphia be trapped and released in a park?
faqs.a: No. Under Pennsylvania's operator rules at 58 Pa. Code Section 147.726(g), a captured raccoon — a codified rabies-vector species in Pennsylvania — must never be released; our crew handles raccoons under those rules and then seals the chimney, soffit, or roof entry and fits a proper cap so the next raccoon cannot use it. What keeps raccoons out of a Philadelphia row home is exclusion, not relocation.

Philadelphia.geographic_features: Delaware River waterfront (working port, marshy edges, and gull and rat food sources), Schuylkill River and Fairmount Park (the largest urban park corridor in the city), Wissahickon Valley Park (deep wooded gorge through the Northwest), Pennypack and Cobbs Creek parks (wooded creek corridors through the Northeast and West)
Philadelphia.housing_era: Philadelphia is a row-home city: brick rowhouses and twins from the 1800s through the 1920s dominate South, North, and West Philadelphia, with postwar twins and singles in the Northeast, stone colonials in Chestnut Hill and Mount Airy, and older apartment blocks scattered throughout. Shared walls, parapet roofs, and aging chimneys give wildlife entries that travel between houses.

Philadelphia.wildlife_intro:
Philadelphia's wildlife calls follow its rowhouses. Norway rats are our steadiest city job, running the alleys, sewers, and restaurant blocks from South Philadelphia to Kensington and the River Wards. Raccoons den in chimneys and parapet rooflines across the Northeast and Northwest, gray squirrels work the street trees and attics of Mount Airy, Germantown, and the Far Northeast, and skunks dig under porches and sheds from West Philadelphia to Pennypack. Big brown bats roost behind shutters and in the rooflines of the older stone and brick stock, and pigeons and starlings fill the vents of commercial blocks and row homes alike. The park corridors matter here: Fairmount Park, the Wissahickon, Pennypack, and Cobbs Creek hold the cover, and the surrounding streets supply the chimneys, decks, and garbage storage animals commute to nightly, so a sealed house on a park-edge block still needs its entries checked every season.

Timing matters in Philadelphia. Raccoon litters arrive in chimneys and attics in spring, bat colonies raise young in the older rooflines through summer — with exclusions held, per Pennsylvania Game Commission guidance, outside the May 15 through August 1 maternity window — and squirrels and rodents make their big push indoors in fall. Even the quiet months are not quiet: overwintering bats wake on warm winter nights, and rats never take a season off in the older districts. Our crew times the work to the animal and the season, removes what is in the structure, and seals every entry we find.
